prize_parts.citation: For the development of palladium-catalyzed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling

statement.case_for: Buchwald-Hartwig amination is a classic enabling method: ligand-controlled palladium catalysis made aryl C-N bond formation general, predictable and scalable, and it is now routine across pharmaceutical, process and materials chemistry. The mechanistic picture (oxidative addition, amine binding, reductive elimination, and how ligand sterics and electronics steer each step) is well established by independent structural and kinetic work. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: two independent groups, Buchwald and Hartwig, drove the general catalyst systems and ligand families, while Kosugi's earlier tin-amide chemistry was a precursor without general scope. Over thirty years of confirmation means there is no maturity risk. It is the kind of method that lets a whole community make what it could not make before.
statement.case_against: The 2010 prize for palladium-catalyzed cross-coupling covers closely related territory, so the committee may judge that the area is already honored and that C-N coupling is an extension of the same idea. It is also a method rather than a new scientific concept, and it has only three first-place or top-three supporters so far, so it may lack the breadth of support needed for a five-vote majority. Kosugi's priority also needs a clear justification in the citation if he is left out.

responses.point: Daniel ranks targeted protein degradation first as a programmable-adaptor modality that reaches proteins inhibitors cannot, with Crews, Deshaies and Handa as the core, while noting that Ciulli, Gray and others make a three-person split contestable.
responses.response: I agree it is a real conceptual advance, and I still rank it third. Handa's cereblon identification is solid structural-biochemical work, and ternary-complex structures do support the mechanism. My reservations are about attribution and timing, not the science. Sakamoto, Kim, Ciulli, Ito and Gray each have a credible claim, and a trio leaves out people whose contributions were decisive for usable molecules. Also, as you concede, no degrader drug is approved yet. I would take it up seriously, but the C-N coupling prize has none of those problems, and if the committee wants a medicine-facing chemistry prize, I would want the molecular-glue and PROTAC parts framed separately before I commit.

responses.point: Johan ranks Buchwald-Hartwig third and values its simplicity and ubiquity, but warns that the 2010 cross-coupling prize may make some colleagues hesitate. He ranks Car-Parrinello second and calls its attribution unusually clean.
responses.response: I take the 2010 overlap seriously and do not dismiss it. My answer is that the 2010 prize rewarded C-C bond formation (Heck, Negishi, Suzuki), whereas C-N coupling needed its own ligand design for hard amine reductive elimination, and that difference is what makes it a separate, general advance. On Car-Parrinello, I agree the two-name attribution is clean and the method is mature, but I would ask how much of its impact is in chemistry rather than condensed-matter physics, and whether experimental users rely on it the way medicinal and process chemists rely on amination. I would not object to it as an alternative, but I do not see it overtaking B038 in demonstrated community use.

responses.point: Peter ranks C-N coupling first as a routine general method in medicinal and process chemistry, with a clear ligand-driven mechanism and a clean two-person attribution of Buchwald and Hartwig.
responses.response: I agree on the science and the pair. Where I would add a qualification is that Kosugi's earlier tin-amide work should be acknowledged in the discussion, since our citation should not suggest nothing came before. I would still keep the prize to the two who made it general. Since you and I are the main supporters, we should state the strongest case against ourselves, which is the 2010 overlap, rather than let others raise it as a surprise.

responses.point: Andrei ranks protein degradation first as a general tool and ranks base editing fourth, naming Liu, Gaudelli and Komor and noting Kondo and Nishida's parallel work.
responses.response: On base editing, I am more comfortable with Liu alone than with the trio. Komor and Gaudelli did the key experiments, but they were trainees in Liu's laboratory, and conceiving the concept is what I would credit. I agree that the deaminase chemistry is interesting and the clinical use is real, but long-term safety data are still accumulating and it builds on the 2020 CRISPR prize. That is why I keep it as an alternative and not my preferred choice.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the 2010 cross-coupling prize as covering C-N coupling, or as leaving room for a separate general method.
Whether Kosugi's priority needs a mention in the citation or discussion even though he is not proposed as a laureate.
Whether protein degradation can be framed with a clean attribution by the time of the final ballot, since it has the broadest opening support.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I am a Stockholm University colleague of the Secretary, Peter Brzezinski, but that does not involve any shortlisted candidate. None of the credited people is a known collaborator, and my own field of electron crystallography is not represented.
